reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour driven by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) infection, classified as a neoplasm although its cause is infective; it presents as violaceous to red-brown macules, plaques, or nodules

Four clinical-epidemiological forms are recognised: classic (older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European origin), endemic (African), iatrogenic (immunosuppressed transplant recipients), and epidemic (AIDS-associated)
AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma is an AIDS-defining illness, so a new diagnosis should prompt HIV testing and assessment of immune status
Lesions often follow skin lines, may be multifocal, and can involve the oral mucosa, gastrointestinal tract, and lungs, sometimes with few or no skin findings
Lymphoedema, particularly of the lower limbs and face, can be prominent and disproportionate to the visible cutaneous disease
Restoring immune function is central to management: antiretroviral therapy in HIV-associated disease and reduction of immunosuppression in transplant-related disease often lead to regression
Localised skin disease may be treated with local measures, while widespread, visceral, or aggressive disease requires systemic chemotherapy under specialist care
Diagnosis is confirmed on biopsy showing proliferating spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, and extravasated red cells, with HHV-8 (LANA) staining
reference.pathophysiology: Kaposi sarcoma arises from HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus) infection of endothelial and progenitor cells, which reprogrammes them towards a spindle-cell, angiogenic phenotype. Viral genes drive cell proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, and stimulate production of angiogenic and inflammatory cytokines, producing the characteristic proliferation of abnormal slit-like vascular channels, spindle cells, and extravasated erythrocytes with haemosiderin deposition. Immune dysfunction, whether from HIV infection or iatrogenic immunosuppression, permits viral reactivation and tumour development, which is why the disease is strongly linked to immunocompromise and often regresses when immunity is restored.
additionalDifferentials: Bacillary angiomatosis (important infective mimic in immunocompromised patients)
Pyogenic granuloma and other vascular proliferations
Melanoma and pigmented lesions (for dark violaceous nodules)
Dermatofibroma and stasis dermatitis changes on the lower legs
additionalInvestigations: Skin or mucosal biopsy with HHV-8 (LANA) immunostaining to confirm the diagnosis
HIV testing and assessment of CD4 count and viral load in newly diagnosed disease
Review of immunosuppressive medication in transplant recipients
Investigation for visceral involvement (for example endoscopy or imaging) when gastrointestinal or pulmonary disease is suspected
Staging assessment to guide whether local or systemic therapy is appropriate
redFlags: New diagnosis prompting HIV testing, as epidemic Kaposi sarcoma is an AIDS-defining condition
Pulmonary involvement causing breathlessness, cough, or haemoptysis, which can be life-threatening
Gastrointestinal disease with bleeding or obstruction
Rapidly progressive or widely disseminated disease requiring urgent oncological input
Extensive lymphoedema causing functional impairment or skin breakdown with secondary infection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the clinical form and immune status: classic Kaposi sarcoma is usually indolent, and iatrogenic and epidemic disease often regress when immune function is restored, whereas disseminated or visceral disease, particularly pulmonary involvement, carries significant morbidity and can be fatal without effective treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to test for HIV when Kaposi sarcoma is diagnosed
Confusing lesions with bacillary angiomatosis in an immunocompromised patient and missing a treatable infection
Overlooking visceral (gastrointestinal or pulmonary) involvement in patients with limited skin disease
Not reviewing and adjusting immunosuppression in transplant-associated disease
Treating aggressively without first optimising immune reconstitution, which alone may induce regression
management: Restore immune function as the cornerstone: antiretroviral therapy in HIV-associated disease and reduction of immunosuppression in transplant recipients, which often induces regression
Treat limited cutaneous disease with local measures such as intralesional chemotherapy, radiotherapy, cryotherapy or topical agents
Use systemic chemotherapy such as liposomal anthracyclines or taxanes for extensive, visceral or rapidly progressive disease
Test for HIV with CD4 count and viral load and stage for visceral involvement to guide therapy
Manage disproportionate lymphoedema and provide symptomatic supportive care
Coordinate multidisciplinary oncology, HIV and transplant medicine input
